controls.statement: Select identity and authentication assurance appropriate to account-compromise harm.
Multifactor enrollment, addition, removal, replacement, and recovery are protected against takeover.
Password handling follows current guidance and does not silently truncate or unexpectedly transform input.
Login defenses address credential stuffing and brute force without creating trivial denial of service.
Login, registration, and recovery responses avoid unnecessary account-existence disclosure.
Enrollment verifies the correct communication channel or identity evidence.
Recovery is no weaker than normal authentication and cannot be redirected through an unverified channel.
Recovery tokens are single-use, short-lived, unpredictable, and stored safely.
Password, authenticator, or recovery changes invalidate appropriate sessions and obsolete recovery material.
Changes to email, phone, payout, identity, recovery, or security settings notify the user and receive enhanced verification where warranted.
Test, dormant, abandoned, and terminated accounts are handled according to policy.
Service accounts do not use inappropriate interactive recovery mechanisms.
Authentication events are audited and suspicious authentication can trigger investigation or step-up controls.
Users can review and revoke relevant sessions and devices where appropriate.
Recovery codes are protected, single-use, and regenerable securely.
Support procedures include social-engineering resistance.
Issuer, audience, signature, algorithm, expiration, nonce, and state are validated as required.
Redirect identifiers are matched exactly according to protocol security requirements.
Authorization-code flows use current proof-key protections where applicable.
Token substitution, replay, and mix-up attacks are addressed.
Automatic account linking cannot merge an attacker's identity with a victim account.
Tokens are limited to minimum required permissions and audiences.
Access and refresh tokens are stored safely.
Refresh-token rotation and reuse detection are used where appropriate.
Revocation, logout, key rotation, metadata refresh, and provider outage behavior are tested.
Authorization is denied by default and enforced server-side at every trusted boundary.

controls.statement: Session identifiers are generated from a cryptographically secure source and have sufficient unpredictability.
Session identifiers are accepted only through intended secure channels.
Browser cookies use secure transport, script-access, cross-site, domain, and path restrictions appropriate to their purpose.
Session identifiers rotate after authentication and privilege changes.
Logout revokes server-side access.
Recovery and credential changes invalidate appropriate sessions.
Persistent login uses separate, appropriately constrained credentials.
State-changing browser operations have CSRF protection.
Tokens validate issuer, audience, subject where needed, type, signature, algorithm, expiration, and not-before time.
Token replay is addressed; refresh credentials are protected against reuse where appropriate.
Tokens and session identifiers do not appear in URLs, referrers, analytics, logs, or error reports.
Client-side token storage is minimized and threat-modeled.
Logout, revocation, and compromise behavior is tested across all components.
File size, count, archive depth, expanded size, dimensions, page count, and processing time are bounded.
File type is determined from content and structure rather than trusting user metadata alone.
Allowed file types are explicitly listed.
User filenames are not trusted as filesystem paths.
Stored names are unpredictable where guessing creates risk.
Untrusted content uses an isolated origin where browser execution could be dangerous.
Access control is checked during upload, listing, preview, transformation, and download.
Download responses use safe content type and disposition behavior and prevent content sniffing.
Image, document, media, archive, and metadata parsers are patched and isolated appropriately.
Temporary, abandoned, failed, and orphaned files are protected and cleaned up.
Retention and deletion rules apply to originals and derived versions.
Processing failures do not expose internal paths or parser details.
Content-moderation and legal controls apply where users can share files.
Tenant context is mandatory at every data, processing, caching, indexing, queueing, file, logging, and administrative boundary.
Tenant isolation is tested in databases, caches, search, queues, files, logs, analytics, backups, exports, and support tools.
Tenant configuration, feature flags, custom code, integrations, and domains cannot affect other tenants.
Cross-tenant timing, error, count, identifier, and existence side channels are minimized.
Support access to a tenant requires authorization, purpose, visibility where appropriate, and audit.
Tenant creation, cloning, migration, split, merge, and deletion preserve isolation and auditability.
Shared templates, catalogs, and global objects cannot leak private tenant data.
Per-tenant data residency, retention, encryption, and compliance commitments are enforced.
Administrative and support interfaces are separately inventoried and threat-modeled.
Strong, preferably phishing-resistant authentication is mandatory for privileged access where risk warrants it.
Privileges are granular and follow least privilege.
Access is just-in-time or time-bounded where practical.
High-impact actions require recent authentication or additional approval where appropriate.
Bulk exports and changes require confirmation, scope preview, authorization, and audit.
Destructive commands have safe limits, dry-run or preview behavior where practical, and clear recovery instructions.
Impersonation is authorized, justified, visibly indicated, time-bounded, and logged.
Sensitive values are masked unless explicitly needed.
Emergency and break-glass access triggers review.
Administrative APIs receive the same or stronger testing as user-facing APIs.
Support tooling cannot bypass tenant, data-residency, retention, or legal boundaries.
Sessions terminate promptly after privilege removal.
Every action is attributable to an individual identity.
Privileged activity is monitored for unusual access, bulk operations, exports, and control changes.
Enterprise federation, domain verification, directory synchronization, provisioning, and deprovisioning are inventoried.

controls.statement: Define each service's cohesive capability, owner, consumers, data authority, and operational objectives.
Split services only when independent ownership, scaling, security, change, or failure isolation justifies the boundary.
Avoid shared databases or mutable internals that bypass service contracts without explicit governance.
Keep business rules in trusted domain logic rather than transport handlers or client code.
Use explicit request, command, query, event, and error contracts.
Validate identity, authorization, tenant, input, quotas, and invariants at every entry point.
Make write operations idempotent where clients or infrastructure can retry.
Keep transaction boundaries aligned to invariants and avoid unbounded remote transactions.
Define timeouts, retries, cancellation, backpressure, and overload behavior.
Make dependency failure degrade safely and observably.
Use structured logging, metrics, traces, health, and audit events tied to user and business outcomes.
Separate readiness from liveness and stop accepting work before shutdown.
Drain, transfer, checkpoint, or safely retry in-flight work during deployment and failure.
Keep configuration, secrets, schema, and deployment versions traceable.
Support backward-compatible rolling deployment where required.
Test service contracts, data behavior, failure, recovery, load, security, and migration independently.
Prevent one tenant, operation, or dependency from exhausting all resources.
Document support, runbook, SLO, capacity, backup, recovery, and retirement obligations.
Avoid exposing internal implementation or database structure as a permanent external contract.
Measure whether the service boundary reduces total coordination and failure cost over time.
Assign every job type, queue, schedule, and dead-letter stream an owner.
Define trigger, input schema, tenant and identity context, priority, deadline, retry, ordering, and completion semantics.
Assume at-least-once execution unless stronger guarantees are proven.
Make side-effecting jobs idempotent or protect effects with deduplication keys.
Persist sufficient state to resume after worker, process, node, or region failure.
Bound attempts, age, execution time, concurrency, queue depth, payload, and resource use.
Use backoff and jitter and prevent retry synchronization.
Distinguish retryable dependency failure from permanent validation, authorization, or business rejection.
Prevent poison work from blocking unrelated work.
Provide dead-letter inspection, privacy protection, alerting, remediation, and safe replay.
Maintain ordering only where the business requires it and account for partitioning and rebalancing.
Protect against overlapping scheduled runs and missed runs.
Define clock, time-zone, daylight-saving, calendar, and catch-up behavior.
Propagate trace, tenant, identity, data classification, and causal context.
Make cancellation and supersession observable and safe.
Avoid embedding mutable large objects or secrets in queue payloads.
Revalidate authorization and current state when delayed work executes.
Monitor queue age, throughput, failures, retries, lag, saturation, and business completion.
Test duplicate, delayed, reordered, lost, corrupt, expired, and partially processed work.
Reconcile authoritative outcomes against job records to detect silent loss or duplication.
Classify each cache or index as disposable, reconstructable, authoritative, or temporarily authoritative.
Define source of truth, key dimensions, freshness, expiry, invalidation, consistency, and reconstruction behavior.
Include identity, tenant, authorization, locale, version, content negotiation, and privacy dimensions in keys where required.
Prevent cache poisoning, key collision, unbounded cardinality, stampede, and eviction of critical entries.
Never serve private or personalized content from a shared cache without correct isolation.
Use negative caching only with safe expiry and authorization semantics.
Make stale serving deliberate and communicate staleness when it affects decisions.
Bound memory, disk, entry size, result size, query complexity, and retention.
Protect search filters, facets, snippets, ranking, and aggregation with the same authorization as source data.
Propagate deletion, correction, legal hold, consent, and tenant changes to derived stores.
Monitor lag, hit rate, miss cost, eviction, index failures, partial updates, and reconstruction duration.
Provide cache bypass and index rebuild procedures for incidents.
Avoid requiring a cache to preserve correctness unless its durability and recovery are engineered accordingly.
Prevent search indexing from exposing secrets, hidden fields, deleted data, or cross-tenant terms.
Test cold start, empty cache, stale entries, concurrent invalidation, failover, and partial indexing.
Reconcile derived counts, documents, and permissions with authoritative data.
Version schemas and ranking behavior for compatible rollout.
Do not use cache as an undocumented communication or locking mechanism.
Make query and ranking behavior explainable enough to diagnose user-visible errors.
Retire obsolete indexes and cached representations with verified cleanup.
